name: Mayangna
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Norwood, Susan 1997. Gramatica de la lengua sumu. Managua: CIDCA (archive.org copy access-restricted); also Palombieri 1967 phonological essai
earlier_scan.note: Grammar exists but text not readable online; Conzemius 1932 survey has no stress statement

new_statements.quote: El acento en sumu es relativamente débil y difícil de distinguir. Puede aparecer en cualquier sílaba (a diferencia del miskito, donde el acento cae generalmente en la primera sílaba). Compárese por ejemplo ililíh "tiburón" en sumu e ílili "tiburón" en miskito.
new_statements.translation: Stress in Sumu is relatively weak and hard to distinguish. It can appear on any syllable (unlike Miskito, where stress generally falls on the first syllable). Compare for example ililíh 'shark' in Sumu and ílili 'shark' in Miskito.
new_statements.citation: Norwood, Susan. 1987. El sumu. Wani (Revista del Caribe Nicaragüense, CIDCA, Managua) 6: 41-48 (digital republication CamJOL 2024, https://camjol.info/index.php/WANI/article/view/19168).
new_statements.locator: p. 43, left column, last paragraph of the phonology section (immediately before the heading MORFOLOGIA); PDF page 3
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (8 pp., CamJOL scan). Rendered PDF page 3 (printed p. 43) at 150 dpi and read it visually: left column, paragraph immediately above the heading MORFOLOGIA reads exactly "El acento en sumu es relativamente débil y difícil de distinguir. Puede aparecer en cualquier sílaba (a diferencia del miskito, donde el acento cae generalmente en la primera sílaba). Compárese por ejemplo ililíh 'tiburón' en sumu e ílili 'tiburón' en miskito." The accent marks (final-syllable í in ililíh, initial í in ílili) are visible on the page image; the extracted text layer ( lines 225-235: "i lil í h... ílili") also carries them, only the tesseract file  drops them. Locator is correct (p. 43, left column, end…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional rule is given: stress is described as weak, hard to hear, and free to fall on any syllable of the word (the one example, ililíh 'shark', is final-stressed, contrasting with initial-stressed Miskito ílili). Convergent older statement: Conzemius 1929 (IJAL 5(1): 74) says Sumu has 'hardly any stress accent at all, all the vowels being nearly equally emphasized' and declines to mark it. Neither source says whether stress is contrastive, so 'lexical-unpredictable' is the closest label; 'no-word-stress-per-source' would fit Conzemius alone.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the only contrast drawn is with Miskito (generally initial).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms (single-word example). The sketch states it is based on the Twahka and Panamaka dialects only (Ulwa not yet studied), i.e. Mayangna proper.
new_statements.identity_note: Norwood's 1987 sketch calls the language 'sumu' but states that only the Twahka and Panamaka dialects had been studied, so the description is of Northern Sumu = Mayangna (maya1285; Panamahka/Twahka dialects of Nicaragua). Conzemius 1929 uses 'Sumu' for all dialects including Ulwa (ulwa1239) and Kukra; Green 1999 (also saved) describes Ulwa, a different language, and must not be attributed to maya1285.

sources.note: p. 43: stress in Sumu is relatively weak and hard to distinguish; it can appear on any syllable (unlike Miskito, where it generally falls on the first syllable); example ililíh 'shark' (Sumu) vs ílili 'shark' (Miskito). Basis of the sketch is explicitly the Twahka and Panamaka dialects (= Mayangna).

sources.citation: Conzemius, Eduard. 1929. Notes on the Miskito and Sumu languages of Eastern Nicaragua and Honduras. International Journal of American Linguistics 5(1): 57-115. DOI 10.1086/463773
sources.note: p. 74 (orthography/phonetics notes): 'In Miskito the stress accent is practically always on the first syllable... In Sumu there is hardly any stress accent at all, all the vowels being nearly equally emphasized. It is very difficult to determine which vowel should bear the stress accent, and for this reason it is not indicated in the following for the different Sumu dialects.' Covers Twahka, Panamaka, Bawihka, Ulwa, Kukra.

sources.note: ULWA (ulwa1239, Southern Sumu), not Mayangna: sec. 4.4 pp. 56-68 gives a weight-sensitive rule for Ulwa (all long vowels stressed; stress on one of the first three syllables; canonical iambic roots stressed on the head/rightmost root syllable). It says nothing about stress in Mayangna; kept only for comparison.
